summary:
Our project LuNaVi is a fast, intuitive 2D web simulator for evaluating landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole. Existing lunar planning tools are slow and visually overwhelming, making rapid scenario comparison difficult. Our application bridges this gap by translating real lunar elevation data and Sun-Earth positions - accounting for Earth’s wobble and the Moon’s airless horizon - into a lightweight map with color-coded layers for sunlight, direct-to-Earth communication, and water ice.
As users drag a landing marker or adjust dates, real-time scales balance science value against survival chances, turning complex orbital angles into everyday indicators like battery power, signal strength, and countdowns to sunset or Earthset, alongside a toggle for detailed engineering metrics. A "Launch Delay" button highlights nearby safe zones when schedules shift, while side-by-side "Mission Passports" let teams compare up to three site-date options in seconds and choose the best variant.

This project is important because rocket delays and competing team priorities constantly reshape lunar missions. LuNaVi accelerates agile decision-making for mission planners while turning complex space mechanics into an accessible, engaging tool for the general public and students.
details:
Introduction

Our project is a single-screen interactive web simulator that turns lunar South Pole mission planning into a fast, intuitive visual trade-off. Instead of forcing users through complex menus or waiting for heavy 3D terrain to load, the app opens directly onto a responsive 2D topographic map of the lunar South Pole with three toggleable color overlays - sunlit zones for solar power (yellow), direct line-of-sight zones for Earth communication (green), and permanently shadowed craters containing water ice (blue).

Users can select notable different locations or enter custom coordinates. As the pin moves, real-time app scales balance science value against survival chances, offering an immediate plain-language verdict on the trade-offs of that spot. Beneath the map, a live HTML5 Canvas horizon view renders the surrounding crater rim silhouette and animates the actual movement of the Sun and Earth across the sky as the user scrubs through a 29.5-day lunar cycle.

To handle real-world schedule shifts, a one-click Launch Delay button demonstrates how moving the landing date alters local shadows and communication windows, automatically highlighting nearby safe zones if the original site falls into darkness. Users can save up to three site-date combinations as Mission Passports to compare battery efficiency, signal strength, and countdowns to sunset or Earthset side by side.

The goal of the project

Existing lunar tools are designed like dense scientific databases - powerful for specialists, yet slow and overwhelming for rapid scenario comparison or public outreach. Our core creative leap was reframing orbital mechanics around the human tension behind every lunar mission: the conflict between scientists who want to explore dark, freezing craters for ice and engineers who need sunlit ridges to keep the lander alive. By translating solar elevation angles and signal geometry into everyday metaphors like battery charge bars and Wi-Fi signal strength, anyone can grasp the engineering stakes in seconds without losing access to underlying technical metrics.

During development, our team carefully accounted for both lunar physics and practical usability constraints. Because the Moon has no atmosphere, there is no twilight - shadows fall abruptly the moment the Sun dips behind a crater ridge, meaning a shift of just a few hundred meters can separate days of continuous power from immediate freezing. We also modeled the South Pole's shallow solar angles alongside Earth's subtle wobble, known as libration, which causes sudden communication blackouts when Earth dips behind distant peaks. Finally, after experiencing how existing 3D lunar portals lag and crash on standard computers, we deliberately eliminated 3D engines, hard scientific termiology and math and also external servers so the application runs instantaneously on any ordinary laptop or classroom device.

Tools, Architecture & Tech Stack

We built the application using Vite and TypeScript as a fast, zero-bloat, single-screen web interface. Every astronomical calculation, horizon obstruction check, and trade-off score runs entirely locally inside the user's browser using pre-processed lunar elevation and ephemeris datasets. The application makes zero backend or external network requests to JPL Horizons, QuickMap, or map tile servers, eliminating API keys, rate limits, and loading delays.

To guarantee smooth performance on everyday laptops, we avoided 3D rendering and WebGL completely. Both the interactive topographic map and the dynamic horizon view - where the Sun and Earth move smoothly across the local mountain profile - are rendered using the native HTML5 Canvas API. All user-created Mission Passports are saved directly on the client side via localStorage, allowing teams and students to save, compare, and revisit scenarios across sessions without creating an account or relying on a database.

Benefits of LuNaVi

LuNaVi bridges the communication gap between science teams, mission engineers, educators, and the general public. For mission planners, it transforms a multi-step data lookup into an instant visual comparison, supporting rapid "what-if" testing during early mission design or sudden rocket launch delays. For teachers, students, and anyone curious about space exploration, it removes intimidating technical barriers and turns abstract celestial mechanics into an engaging interactive puzzle that clearly shows why returning to the Moon's South Pole is one of humanity's most delicate engineering balancing acts.
